elements.text: Guys, BIP 143 has a funny detail, what do you think of it?

When you make an endorsement for a segwit input witness to spend a P2WPKH output, the signtext part for the pubkey script of the output to be consumed is this:

"The item 5: For P2WPKH witness program, the scriptCode is 0x1976a914{20-byte-pubkey-hash}88ac."

I.e. the P2*PKH* pubkeyscript template (DUP HASH160 hash EQUALVERIFY CHECKSIG).

What sense do you make of this choice?

At least on first sight it looks a bit assymetrical to me.

Gmaxwell provided the following clarifications which I feel didn't clarify at all also:

"it is the implied pubkey.

Because that is the actual public key in use.

in the sense that that is the script that the network is actually validating.

In general, it's advistable that signatures actually commit to their conditions, so they can't be rebound.

Otherwise, I could potentially trick an application into signing for X when it's really signing for Y.

(like if a user reused a key in different applications, foolishly)

you can just think of it as the stored spk being compressed.

the txout effectively is storing a compressed representation of the actual script. The actual script is OP_DUP OP_HASH160 x OP_EQUALVERIFY OP_CHECKSIG.

but it wastes some blockchain space to encode all that, so instead only a version and x gets stored.

The P2WPKH is just a compact encoding for the witness script I pasted above. You sign the actual script, rather than the compact encoding."



Thoughts?

the txout effectively is storing a compressed representation of the actual script. The actual script is OP_DUP OP_HASH160 x OP_EQUALVERIFY OP_CHECKSIG.

but it wastes some blockchain space to encode all that, so instead only a version and x gets stored.

The P2WPKH is just a compact encoding for the witness script I pasted above. You sign the actual script, rather than the compact encoding."

elements.text:
Ah, Maxwell clarified additionally eventually.

What I understand him to mean is that, conceptually P2WPKH is P2PKH just with the signature in the witness instead.

P2WPKH's nature is such that, when you endorse spending a P2WPKH output, then the pubkey script regarded is, conceptually, DUP HASH160 hash EQUALVERIFY CHECKSIG, and for this reason that's what an endorsement in a witness should sign.



(He then goes on to make a separate point that the native P2WPKH pubkey script can be seen as "compressed" in the sense that OP_0 PUSHDATA [20B] is 22 bytes while DUP HASH160 hash EQUALVERIFY CHECKSIG is 25 bytes.)

I guess that brought final clarification to it.

elements.text:
Hello Everyone

I posted to this Slack channel a while ago about the research I am currently conducting related to the usability of Bitcoin APIs. As I had mentioned, I am specifically looking into libbitcoin. This mainly for two reasons: on the one hand, C++ is the programming language I am most familiar with. On the other hand, the other noteworthy C++ implementation, i.e. Bitcoin Core, does not offer a C++ API per se (but an RPC JSON API, as I am sure all of you know). Although I am also planning to evaluate Bitcoin Core's C++ implementation if time allows, my research is primarily focusing on libbitcoin.

I am studying for a Master in Computer and Information Security at the University of Liverpool and this is my final research project. This is an online programme; I am actually living in Switzerland. My project requires me to have an expert review my findings. I am, therefore, asking if one of the libbitcoin contributors among you would be willing to spend one to two hours of your time to review the relevant chapters of my dissertation and provide written feedback for me to cite in the dissertation report. My dissertation is due 6th of March 2019. I am planning to finish the chapters related to the libbitcoin API evaluation sometime in January 2019 but should be able to provide a draft by the end of the year. Your review would be required to reach me towards the end of January 2019.

While I cannot offer any compensation for your help, I can offer to send pull requests related to any of my findings for you to merge or ignore at your discretion. Please let me know if you have further questions about my research.

Thanks! Philipp

As for the methodology, I am evaluating libbitcoin's API in relation to a subset of the API usability heuristics and guidelines defined by Mosqueira-Rey et al. (see reference further down). To help with this, I have implemented some of the guidelines in a static code analysis tool built using Clang Libtooling. As my hypothesis was (or is) that supporting usable security in Bitcoin APIs would help to protect against potential vulnerabilities in SW that uses such APIs, I had initially planned to analyse client SW that uses libbitcoin. However, I have not found many open source applications suitable for analysis, so I am focusing on the API and its usability now. I still have to analyse its use, as this is what my proposal says I will do, but I'll have to do with what's available, which is basically what comes with libbitcoin, i.e. libbitcoin-explorer, libbitcoin-node and libbitcoin-server. I think I found one or two others.



Mosqueira-Rey, Eduardo, David Alonso-Ríos, Vicente Moret-Bonillo, Isaac Fernández-Varela, and Diego Álvarez-Estévez. “A Systematic Approach to API Usability: Taxonomy-Derived Criteria and a Case Study.” Information and Software Technology 97 (May 2018): 46–63.

Messed around with clang-format a bit. It won’t conform 100% with the style in libbitcoin. Some rules that we just configure it for are

1. can’t force breaks before inheritance lists, unless they hit 80 col limit
2. it will put a break before the first parameter if call or function declaration exceeds 80 col limit
3. can’t config it to put a new line before lambda expressions

Am sure there are some other rules it breaks too.

As pros, it has excellent support for VS and emacs. For VS you can format a file explicitly or automatically on save. There is a ClangFormat extension for VS Code since last year.
